newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax reform raises hopes, fears for coalition.
newsitem.headline: German tax reform raises hopes, fears for coalition.

text.p: Germany's planned tax reform has raised enormous hopes it will cure many of the country's woes, but the threat that tax cuts will be watered down looms ominously over Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition.

Dubbed the reform of the century, Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to cut the top tax rate to 39 percent from 53 percent will run into stiff headwind from lobbies and countless other interest groups whose tax breaks face elimination.

The tax reform proposals were quickly criticised by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and taxpayer groups because an increase in value-added tax is needed to finance the income tax cuts. The SPD could block significant parts of the measure through its control of the upper house of parliament.
Even members of Kohl's Christian Democrats have slammed the reform proposal because they say it fails to go far enough, a sentiment that found an echo in many newspaper commentaries.

"The final judgement will be that the politicians never tried a true reform because they are too weak..." said the Sueddeutsche Zeitung newspaper on Thursday. "Theo Waigel has presented us with a touch-up job rather than a reform."
Analysts said that expectations had been wound so high that if the reform were to ultimately fail, such a debacle could pose a serious threat to Kohl's centre-right coalition.

"The reputation of the coalition is now dependent on whether the reform succeeds," said Thomas Mayer, chief economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt. He lamented the fact that the law is not due to take effect until 1999.
"So many hopes have been pinned to the reform that if it fails, you can kiss this government good-bye," he added.
"There will be endless wrangling over the cuts in write-offs. If they start watering it down, there is a risk the coalition will collapse."

The months of public discussion have awakened enormous hopes among voters that their tax rates will drop sharply and their take home pay will rise. That, they have been told, will spur economic growth and reduce unemployment.

"This is a success for the coalition," said Hermann Otto Solms, parliamentary leader of the FDP. "The reform will be good for those looking for employment because it is a decisive step toward improving Germany's competitive position."
In addition to cutting the top rate of income tax, a new low rate of 15 percent for low earners would be introduced.

Among the unpopular suggestions to help make up for lost revenues are a VAT increase -- one or two percentage points is a matter of dispute -- and new taxes on some pensions and life insurance policies.

"Raising the VAT in order to finance an income tax cut is absolutely the wrong way to go," said Karl-Heinz Daeke, president of the Taxpayers' Association. "The government will be taking out of one pocket what it puts in the other."

Waigel also wants to close the tax code's many loopholes but lobbies are fighting back. His own Christian Social Union (CSU) party, afraid of losing its majority at Bavaria's next state election, is baulking at cutting breaks for commuters because so many rural voters there have long drives to work.

Waigel has deflected calls to resign. The criticism has not hit Kohl yet, but the frequent talk about the general election almost two years away shows how much CDU politicians see riding on the reform.

Kohl's centre-right coalition, now in its record 14th year in office, is weak enough already. The latest Emnid poll showed support running at 43 percent compared to 48 percent for the opposition Social Democrats and Greens together.
